Monolinguals, not familiar with tones or even recognizing that there are tones superimposed, performed similarly on every word, whether they matched or mismatched.  No differences were found in either recognition or production, suggesting that the supra-segmental aspect of tone does not act as competing information in monolinguals as it does in bilinguals.

The results regarding current exposure to Mandarin radio and music seem to suggest that more current exposure to listening in Mandarin might make one more aware of the importance of tones in listening for meaning.  There may be a few reasons for this; it may be the case that the increased exposure to passive Mandarin listening, either in the form of talk radio or music, increases the sensitivity to Mandarin tones, thus leading to a greater effect on processing.  In addition, those who listen to Mandarin radio and music may identify more with their Chinese culture and thus keep Mandarin more active all the time, even when performing an English task.  This interaction between listening and tone perception in language is an area which could be looked at more in depth in future studies.

From the results of our study, we seem to have preliminary evidence that even if bilinguals’ word choice is not ultimately affected by the superimposition of tone, their processing does seem to be affected in some way, which makes them different from monolinguals.  This provides support for previous studies which suggested that Chinese listeners incorporate both segmental and supra-segmental information into their lexical representations, whereas English listeners do not take this supra-segmental information into account.¹⁷  Future studies might further explore this relationship by measuring reaction times in a more objective, non-subject regulated method, by monitoring electrical activity in areas of the brain using electrodes, as physical evidence of when brain activity starts and stops.  We did not find the expected difference in word choice between bilinguals and monolinguals, perhaps due to methodological issues, which leaves possibilities open for future studies in this area.  One possibility includes attempts to increase the strength of Mandarin activation during the study, either by choosing participants who are more proficient in Mandarin than English (therefore they would choose to activate their more proficient language) or by activating Mandarin through the experimental procedure and communication, while keeping the actual English experiment intact.

Taking the results of this study in conjunction with previous studies, we have evidence suggesting that Mandarin-English bilinguals process English differently than English monolinguals due to the presence of supra-segmental information.  Even if we did not find evidence supporting the hypothesis that word choice would be affected, findings that processing differences appeared in the reaction time data suggest that there is some effect of supra-segmental information taken from Mandarin when processing English.
